analytic.title: Work in Progress: Reducing WCET Estimation by Increasing the Number of Persistent Blocks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Safety-critical systems depend on the temporal guarantees provided by schedulability analysis of hard real-time systems. Worst-case execution time analysis (WCET) is a necessary component in schedulability analysis of hard real-time systems. A central goal of WCET analysis is to produce a tight bound, since tighter bounds (generally) increase the schedulability of a system. Cache memory is an impediment to tight WCET analysis due to the variability it introduces into task systems. However, static modification of memory access patterns within mutable objects may increase cache-hits and reduce WCET. Herein, a mechanism for modifying and analyzing hard real-time tasks is proposed. The proposed mechanism leverages existing persistence analysis to identify sets of blocks to retain in cache during execution. Retention guarantees persistence, resulting in tighter WCET analysis.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Safety-critical systems are systems where operational failure may lead to harm or loss of property or personal safety. Such systems, including flight, aerospace, and autonomous vehicles, are typically modeled as hard real-time systems. For these systems, ensuring temporal guarantees is important for operational safety.

To provide temporal guarantees, the worst-case execution time (WCET) of a task must be known. WCET analysis [1] purports to calculate an upper bound on the execution time of a task given a specific hardware platform. Paramount to WCET analysis is the calculation of a safe upper bound, one that is greater than or equal to any possible execution duration given any possible input. Of almost equal importance is the calculation of a tight upper bound, a bound is said to be tighter than another when it is smaller while remaining safe.

WCET analysis is incorporated into schedulability analysis, which determines if all tasks running on a platform will always meet their deadlines. For hard real-time systems without anomalies [2], reducing WCETs increases schedulability. Further, in embedded systems powered by capacitors and energy harvesters, the execution of tasks is responsible for up to 80% of energy consumption [3]. Existing techniques [4] for meeting temporal guarantees while minimizing energy consumption depend on WCET values, where a lower WCET decreases energy consumption. Thus, lower WCET values may increase schedulability and will decrease energy usage.

Persistence analysis [5] aims to incorporate hit and miss behavior into WCET analysis by categorizing cache blocks as persistent. A persistent cache block misses once and is guaranteed to hit for all other memory accesses. To incorporate persistence analysis into WCET analysis, blocks that persist contribute exactly one miss for all memory accesses, compared to non-persistent blocks which contribute a miss for every memory access. Therefore, increasing the number of persistent blocks during persistence analysis [6] will decrease WCET values.

The proposed mechanism for increasing the number of persistent blocks is guided by the concept of rejuvenating cache values. By inserting a LOAD instruction for a memory block present in the cache, the replacement policy information is updated, ensuring that block will remain in the cache. Repeatedly inserting LOADs will rejuvenate a memory block, guaranteeing its presence in the cache. By doing so, persistence analysis may increase the number of persistent cache blocks. The replacement policy considered is least recently used (LRU) and rejuvenation is restricted to elements that map to the data cache (rather than instruction cache). As a software-based mechanism, no hardware support is required for the proposed approach. The central contributions of the approach are:

1) Rejuvenation of cached values to increase the number of persistent blocks 2) A heuristic for selecting cached values to rejuvenate based upon current state-of-the-art persistence analysis [6] Contributions are presented in the following sections. Section II presents the task model, processor architecture, and cache architecture. Section III provides a brief background on the underlying persistence analysis. Section IV outlines the heuristic rejuvenation placement algorithm and analysis. Section V summaries related work in persistence analysis. Section VI concludes the presentation and outlines future opportunities.

div.head: II. MODEL
div.p: To simplify the presentation, the following assumptions are made of the system being analyzed and the underlying architecture. Given the focus on WCET calculation, only a single task τ is considered. The task executes on a single processor with separate instruction and data caches. Being limited to refreshing only data cache values, the organization and behavior of the instruction cache is omitted. The data cache has µ cache sets and each cache set has n ways, where n ≥ 2. This work considers the LRU replacement policy since it is extensively studied. Each cache block holds exactly one word.

Further assumptions are made regarding execution of instructions. Instruction execution times are separable into the number of cycles required to load each instruction and the number of cycles required to execute the instruction. For simplicity in explanation, this paper considers that executing any instruction requires the same constant cycles per instruction (CPI) denoted by I. The number of cycles required to load values into the data cache, which is referred to as the block reload time, is denoted by B. The B and I values are representative, where I < B. Experimentally [7], for limited architectures, the values differ by approximately 2,000 cycles when I is near 1.

The processor provides a LOAD instruction. The paper considers that the load instruction places a block of main memory into the cache. Doing so updates the replacement policy of the cache set which the block belongs to. If the value is absent from the cache, LOAD would consume B + I cycles to complete. When the block is present in the cache, LOAD requires I cycles, assuming the memory controller resets the age of the block to most recently used [8].

To illustrate the impact of a LOAD instruction upon the age of a block, consider a single cache set, C, with an LRU cache that is 4-way associative. Before an access to B 5 the ordered set of values in the cache set are C = {B 2 , B 4 , B 1 , B 3 }, where B 2 is the youngest and B 3 is the oldest. Access to B 5 evicts B 3 and loads B 5 into the cache. Inserting a LOAD to B 3 before access to B 5 will make it the youngest in the cache set. C = {B 3 , B 2 , B 4 , B 1 }, resulting in B 1 's eviction when B 5 is accessed.

div.head: III. BACKGROUND ON PERSISTENCE ANALYSIS
div.p: This proposed approach relies upon persistence analysis, specifically the exact persistence analysis proposed in [6]. This section presents an overview of exact persistence analysis.

Conflict sets are fundamental to exact persistence analysis, they are constructed and updated per memory block. Given a program point, a conflict set of a block B i is a set of distinct memory blocks, mapping to the same cache set as B i , accessed on an execution path. The set of conflict sets, representing distinct paths through the task, is denoted by Ŝ(B i ).

For a memory block B i , Ŝ(B i ) is empty until an access of B i . When any block B j that maps to B i 's cache set is accessed, Ŝ(B i ) is updated according to Equation (1). When B j is not B i the conflict sets are expanded to include B j . When B j is B i the conflict sets are reduced to a single set containing B i .

A memory block B i is said to be persistent if all memory accesses excluding the first access to block B i result in a cache hit. Stated equivalently, the cardinality of every conflict set is less than or equal to the associativity of the cache.

The proposed approach to reducing WCET values by rejuvenating memory blocks is divided into two parts. First, the mechanism that inserts LOADs to rejuvenate cached values, guaranteeing their persistence. Second, the approach to selecting which values to rejuvenate. This section presents the mechanism. Following sections present the challenges of selection and an initial heuristic for selection.

div.head: A. Guaranteeing Persistence Through Rejuvenation
div.p: The mechanism for rejuvenating a target block B i relies upon the persistence analysis of the task. Across the task, LOADs to block B i are inserted at each program pointbetween the first and last access to B i -where any conflict set of B i has cardinality greater than the associativity of the cache; given by Equation (3). 2) Move all incident edges of ρ v to ρ u , (ρ t , ρ v ) → (ρ t , ρ u ) 3) Insert an edge (ρ u , ρ v ) accessing B i These abstract steps represent the practical operation of inserting a LOAD B i instruction into the executable before any instruction that would increase any of B i 's conflict sets beyond the associativity of the cache. Figure 2 illustrates the modification of a task to guarantee B 1 's persistence for a 3way associative cache. The light gray program point ρ v in Figure 2a becomes the blue point in Figure 2b. The green point in Figure 2b corresponds to ρ u in the steps listed above. Persistence analysis produces, for each memory block, a set of conflict sets at each program point. The proposed approach aims to reduce the WCET of a task. To meet the goal of the proposed approach, consideration must be given, simultaneously, to all blocks that map to a task set. The following challenges expand upon the need to consider all blocks within a set simultaneously.
Challenge of Occlusion: The rejuvenation of a block B i may prevent another block B j from being persistent. When persisting B i precludes B j from persisting, it is said that B i occludes B j .

Challenge of Impact: Given two blocks that do not persist, B i and B j , determining which contributes more significantly than the other depends on the program structure and accesses of the blocks. A block B i may be accessed many times along paths that do not contribute to the WCET, while a block B j may be accessed few times along paths that contribute to the WCET.

Challenge of Limits: For a given associativity n, at most n blocks persist at each program point. These three challenges motivate the need to select n blocks simultaneously among all those accessing a cache set to find an optimal solution. As a work-in-progress, this approach addresses the first challenge of occlusion directly. The other challenges are not addressed with an exact solution; rather, an initial heuristic is suggested.

div.head: C. Persistent Block Selection
div.p: Addressing the Impact Challenge: The heuristic decision on which blocks to rejuvenate is derived from the impact on the WCET analysis. For blocks classified as non-persistent, each access to it costs B + I. For blocks that persist, the first memory access to it costs B + I, while the subsequent accesses cost I. Rejuvenating blocks that are accessed more often than others would intuitively have the greatest reduction in the WCET. Thus, the heuristic approach is to prioritize the persistence of blocks according to their number of accesses.
Addressing the Limits Challenge: As an initial solution, the n highest priority blocks that reduce the WCET are considered for rejuvenation within the program.

Addressing the Occlusion Challenge: The proposed approach addresses the challenge of occlusion by loading multiple blocks on a rejuvenated edge. Figure 3 illustrates the behavior for a 3-way associative cache. Consider the original program structure in Fig. 2a, where B 2 is classified as persistent. During rejuvenation of B 1 , to ensure persistence of B 2 , both blocks B 2 and B 1 are loaded on the rejuvenated edge (shown between the green and blue program points). Specifically, B 2 's LOAD must precede B 1 's LOAD. Examining Figure 3, the conflict sets of B 2 are less than or equal to 3 at all program points. Thus B 2 persists without impacting B 1 's conflict sets or persistence. Pseudocode for the approach is presented as Algorithm 1. The algorithm accepts the associativity of the cache, n, and the prioritized ordering of the set of blocks accessed, B, as input. The approach iteratively attempts to rejuvenate up to n blocks from B. During each iteration, the heuristic determines if rejuvenating the current block b reduces the WCET of the task. If so, the rejuvenate modification is maintained. Otherwise, the rejuvenate modification is REVERTED for b.

div.head: V. RELATED WORK
div.p: Persistence analysis exists within the larger category of static analysis, which includes cache and WCET analysis [9]. Other forms of static cache analysis include cache related preemption delay (CRPD) [10]- [12], coherency and false

div.p: sharing [13]. These static methods aim to bound interference and the impact of cache memory on real-time systems, while this approach proposes the modification of executable objects to benefit WCET values.

PREM [14] is another approach that combines static analysis and executable modification. It is both a model of execution and a scheduling algorithm that divides tasks into load and execute phases for the purpose of limiting inter-task cache interference. The method proposed in this work takes the perspective of positively impacting the performance of a single task without explicit region creation.

This work relies upon persistence analysis, an approach that enhanced must analysis [15]. Must analysis focuses on determining if a memory block will always be cached at a specific location. In 2018, Reineke provided a comprehensive survey of persistence analysis [16]; categorizing and comparing the seminal approaches of Block-CS [17], [18], C-Must [15], and Global-CS [19]- [22].

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: At the time of writing, the authors are unaware of any prior efforts to alter the persistence classification of memory blocks to reduce WCET. The proposed mechanism and heuristic aim to reduce, but not optimize, which blocks to grant a guarantee of persistence. To address the challenges of occlusion, impact, and limits, future work will focus on two areas. First, the consideration of alternative rejuvenation mechanisms. Second, the simultaneous selection of blocks to persist to optimize WCET values on a per cache set basis.

In the future, other replacement policies will be considered. Further extensions of this work will include improvements to the initial solutions to all challenges. Rejuvenation in different scopes used in persistence analysis will also be considered in the future. Rejuvenation may introduce overhead (additional cache misses) on instruction caches due to the increased program size. The challenge of balancing the overhead and the benefit of rejuvenation will be addressed in the future.
